subject: Agriculture
title: Gene Banks and Preservation
description: A quick, practical guide to Gene Banks and Preservation.

hook.text: The Svalbard Global Seed Vault holds 1.2 million seed samples inside an Arctic mountain. It's agriculture's backup drive.

buildup.text: Humans have cultivated 7,000 plant species for food. Today, just three—rice, wheat, corn—provide 50% of all calories.

discovery.text: Gene banks preserve wild crop relatives with traits—drought tolerance, disease resistance—that modern crops bred out.

twist.text: Syria's gene bank in Aleppo was partially destroyed in the civil war. Its backup seeds in Svalbard saved the collection.

climax.text: Climate change will demand new crop traits. Gene banks hold the genetic diversity that breeders will need.

punchline.text: 1.2 million seeds in a frozen vault. Humanity's insurance against the unknown.

quiz.question: How many seed samples does the Svalbard Global Seed Vault hold?

details.summary: Gene banks preserve seeds, tissue samples, and genetic material from crop varieties and wild relatives. This topic covers the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, national gene banks, and why genetic diversity is critical for future food security.
details.whyItMatters: Modern agriculture relies on a narrow genetic base. Gene banks safeguard the diversity needed to breed crops that can withstand new diseases, pests, and climate conditions.
takeaways: The Svalbard vault holds over one million seed samples as a global backup
Wild crop relatives contain genes for drought and disease resistance
Loss of crop genetic diversity threatens humanity's ability to adapt food systems

faq.question: What is a gene bank and why is it important?
faq.answer: A gene bank is a facility that stores seeds, plant tissues, or DNA from diverse crop varieties and their wild relatives. These collections preserve genetic traits that breeders may need to develop crops resistant to future threats.

faq.question: How does the Svalbard Global Seed Vault protect crop diversity?
faq.answer: Located deep inside an Arctic mountain in Norway, the vault stores duplicate samples from gene banks worldwide as a backup against natural disasters, wars, or equipment failures that could destroy other collections.
